title: Binary conversion and addition
starter: An 8-bit counter reads 11111111. What do you think happens when it counts one more?
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: Place values
facts: Each bit in an 8-bit number has a place value: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
Add the place values above every 1 to get the denary number.
The largest 8-bit number is 255, when every bit is 1.
stations.challenge: What is 11111111 in denary, and why?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Each bit in an 8-bit number has a place value: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
Also credit: Add the place values above every 1 to get the denary number.

questions.q: What is the largest number that 8 bits can store?

stations.name: Denary to binary
facts: Work from the left: does 128 fit? If yes, write 1 and subtract it.
Check by adding your place values back up.
stations.challenge: Convert 173 into 8-bit binary and show your working.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Work from the left: does 128 fit? If yes, write 1 and subtract it.
Also credit: Carry on down through 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1.

stations.name: MSB and LSB
facts: The most significant bit (MSB) is the leftmost bit: it has the largest place value.
The least significant bit (LSB) is the rightmost: place value 1.
Changing the MSB changes the number by 128; changing the LSB changes it by 1.
stations.challenge: Explain the terms most significant bit and least significant bit.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: The most significant bit (MSB) is the leftmost bit: it has the largest place value.
Also credit: The least significant bit (LSB) is the rightmost: place value 1.

questions.q: Which bit is the most significant bit?
questions.a: The leftmost bit, with the place value 128

questions.q: Changing the least significant bit from 0 to 1 changes the number by how much?

stations.name: Binary addition
facts: Add column by column from the right, just like denary.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Add column by column from the right, just like denary.
Also credit: 0+0 = 0; 0+1 = 1; 1+1 = 10, so write 0 and carry 1.

questions.q: Add these two binary numbers. Tick the overflow box only if the answer needs a 9th bit.

stations.name: Overflow
facts: If the answer needs a 9th bit, it can't be stored: this is an overflow error.
The stored answer is wrong, which can crash a program or corrupt data.
stations.challenge: What can happen to the most significant bit when you add two binary numbers?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: 8 bits can only hold 0 to 255.
Also credit: If the answer needs a 9th bit, it can't be stored: this is an overflow error.

questions.q: Add these two binary numbers, and tick the overflow box if the answer needs a 9th bit.
questions.a: 11110000 + 00010100 = 00000100 (240 + 20 = 260), and the answer needs a 9th bit, so an overflow error occurs
The result of a calculation is too large for the number of bits available

stations.name: Why it matters
facts: More bits means bigger numbers: 16 bits reach 65,535.
Programs must choose a data type big enough for the values they'll hold.
Famous failures, including a rocket, have been caused by overflow.
stations.challenge: Suggest a situation where an overflow error could be dangerous.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: More bits means bigger numbers: 16 bits reach 65,535.
Also credit: Programs must choose a data type big enough for the values they'll hold.

questions.q: How can a programmer avoid overflow errors?
questions.a: Use a data type with enough bits for the largest possible value

questions.q: How many values can 16 bits represent?

final.name: Final challenge: convert and add

questions.q: Add these two binary numbers, and tick the overflow box if needed.
questions.a: 11000110 + 01010111 = 00011101 (198 + 87 = 285), and the answer needs a 9th bit, so an overflow error occurs

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
